candidates.angle: yam, whom, is the object of disturbance
dhīram, steadfast, names the one who stays even through pleasure and pain
amṛtatvāya, for immortality, names the goal of the steadfast

angle_en: Dhiram: the steadfast person who stays even through pleasure and pain
angle_hi: धीरं: वह अडिग व्यक्ति जो सुख-दुख में समान रहता है

en.intro: The previous verse said to endure heat and cold. But how? Listen to how Krishna names the person who can do it.
en.notice: Listen to the word dhiram, steadfast. It names the person who stays even through pleasure and pain, and that steadiness is what makes him fit for freedom.
en.next: Krishna now asks you to look at the boundary between what is real and what is not.
en.meaning: The wise person who is not shaken by these, and remains equal in pain and pleasure, becomes fit for freedom.

hi.intro: पिछले श्लोक में कहा गया था कि सुख-दुख सहो। लेकिन यह कैसे? सुनिए, श्रीकृष्ण किस व्यक्ति का नाम लेते हैं जो इसे कर सकता है।
hi.meaning: हे पुरुषों में श्रेष्ठ अर्जुन, जिस धीर पुरुष को ये सुख-दुख विचलित नहीं करते और जो दोनों में समान रहता है, वही मोक्ष के योग्य होता है।
hi.notice: यहाँ 'धीरं' (अडिग) पर ध्यान दीजिए। यह उस व्यक्ति को दर्शाता है जो सुख-दुख दोनों में समान रहता है, और यही स्थिरता उसे मोक्ष के योग्य बनाती है।
hi.next: अब श्रीकृष्ण आपसे यह देखने को कहते हैं कि जो सत्य है और जो असत्य, उसकी सीमा क्या है।

issues: borrowed: "Listen to the word yena, whom. It points to a person, not a feeling or a situation, and that person is the one who stays even through pain and pleasure to find freedom." (The script mentions 'yena' (whom), but the Sanskrit of this verse uses 'yam' (whom) and 'hi' (indeed), not 'yena'. More importantly, the phrase 'to find freedom' is borrowed from the fixed English meaning of the next verse (verse 16), which discusses the boundary of real and unreal, not this verse.)

unsupported: "Here 'yam' (whom) pay attention. It points to a person, not a feeling or a situation, and that person is the one who stays even through pain and pleasure to find freedom." (The script claims that 'yam' points to a person, not a feeling or situation. However, 'yam' is an accusative pronoun referring to the object of the verb 'vyathayanti' (disturb). The grammar is about the object of disturbance, not a grammatical distinction between persons and feelings.)
